question: On July 15, 2008, Phys.org published an article about a catastrophe. Find the explosive force of this catastrophe according to Encyclopedia Britannica, then find the name of the US nuclear test that had the same yield. Your answer should only be the last word of the name of the test.

history.name: user
history.content: On July 15, 2008, Phys.org published an article about a catastrophe. Find the explosive force of this catastrophe according to Encyclopedia Britannica, then find the name of the US nuclear test that had the same yield. Your answer should only be the last word of the name of the test.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content:
Task: Identify the catastrophe in the July 15, 2008 Phys.org article, get its explosive force per Encyclopedia Britannica, then match that yield to a US nuclear test and return only the last word of the test’s name.
Plan:
- Confirm which catastrophe the Phys.org article covers.
- Retrieve Britannica’s stated explosive force for that event.
- Find a US nuclear test with the same yield.
- Output only the last word of the test name.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: WebSurfer, locate the Phys.org article published on July 15, 2008 and identify the catastrophe and its context.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Search completed: Found Phys.org article dated July 15, 2008 titled “Tunguska catastrophe: Evidence of acid rain supports ...” It discusses the 1908 Tunguska event over Siberia and reports isotopic evidence (nitrogen/carbon) indicating acid rain caused by a high-energy atmospheric explosion. Catastrophe identified: Tunguska event.

history.name: Assistant
history.content: Next, we need Britannica’s stated explosive force for the Tunguska event. WebSurfer, please search Britannica for “Tunguska event explosive force TNT” and capture the explicit yield wording.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
Britannica results:
- Page A (Tunguska event overview): “The energy of the explosion is estimated to have been equivalent to the explosive force of as much as 15 megatons of TNT.”
- Page B (related article): Mentions the range “about 10–15 megatons of TNT,” indicating uncertainty and a span.
So Britannica presents either an upper-bound phrasing (as much as 15 Mt) or a range (10–15 Mt).

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Verification policy: Because Britannica presents a range or an upper bound, we will standardize on the conservative lower bound for precise matching to avoid overstating. Adopt 10 megatons as the definitive Britannica explosive force. To validate, we will consider any secondary source that corroborates the existence of the 10–15 range as sufficient confirmation. Sign-off criteria: If Britannica shows a range including 10 and a secondary source also shows a similar range, we accept 10 Mt as the verified figure.

history.name: Assistant
history.content:
Verification report:
- Britannica Page B indicates a 10–15 Mt range.
- Secondary source (Wikipedia summary) also states a 10–15 Mt range.
- Criteria met. Approved: 10 megatons is the verified Britannica explosive force for Tunguska.
Proceeding with 10 Mt as the matching target.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: WebSurfer, find the US nuclear test with the same yield (use 10 Mt, and if necessary round to the nearest whole megaton to align). Report the test name and yield.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
Search results for US test near 10 Mt:
- Ivy Mike (Operation Ivy): Yield approximately 10.4 megatons of TNT; commonly cited as ~10 Mt class.
- Castle Romeo: ~11 Mt (exceeds 10 Mt).
Selecting Ivy Mike as the closest match to 10 Mt (rounding 10.4 down to 10 for equivalence). Full name: Ivy Mike.

mistake_reason: At step 6, the orchestrator imposed a flawed verification policy that forcibly standardized Britannica’s explosive force to the conservative lower bound (10 Mt) despite Britannica’s explicit wording emphasizing an upper bound (“as much as 15 megatons”) and a range (10–15 Mt). This defective verification logic treated the lower bound as the definitive value and set sign-off criteria that only required overlapping ranges rather than confirming the specific Britannica figure. The Assistant then approved this erroneous verification at step 7, leading the team to match the wrong yield (10 Mt) and select Ivy Mike instead of the correct 15 Mt Castle Bravo. This matches FM-3.3 (Incorrect Verification): failure to adequately validate crucial information, applying flawed criteria, and explicitly approving an incorrect result.
